content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper shows how a multi-exit strategy in conjunction with a fairness-aware optimization can improve metrics such as equalized odds while maintaining accuracy in classification tasks. The proposed algorithm chooses which exit point to use during inference by selecting the exit with highest confidence (a previously proposed techniques by Kaya et al). At each exit point a classifier is trained by combining a traditional classification loss L_t with a term that minimizes the the equalized odds discrepancy L_s. Specifically equalized odd is implemented as the delta between true positive rates (between two sub-populations) and also the delta between false positive rates: L_s = |TPR_1 -TPR_2 + FPR_1 - FPR_2|. All classifiers (including the traditional last one) are trained together where each exit point loss term is weighted by coefficient alphas that are a hyper-parameters the user sets: \alpha_i (L_s + \lambda  L_t ) for each exit point i.

Results are shown on CelebA and UTK Faces datasets. On both datasets the comparison shows the results of a set of algorithms ( LNL (Kim et al., 2019), HSIC (Quadrianto et al., 2019), MFD (Jung et al., 2021), and FSCL (Park et al., 2022)) and how their accuracy and equalized odds change when the proposed multi-exit strategy is applied to the original algorithm. Results show that the equalized odd metric is always improved when adopting the proposed strategy, while the accuracy is sometime improved sometime degraded (at most improved by 5.8% and degraded by 3%).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
- Simple and effective technique to improve equalized odds.

Weaknesses (should be addressed to upgrade score)
- Results should be presented for larger use cases and settings:
    - Results are limited to 1 single fairness measure (Equalized Odds) and binary predictions. Especially when using the confidence of the classifier as exit strategy the presence of a more complex outcome (not just binary) could lead more frequently to calibration issues, which in turn could lead to the wrong exit choice. Such effect should be evaluated on accuracy and fairness.
- Some experiments seem inconclusive, or perhaps conclusions should be explained more clearly. For example I am not sure what the take away from the experiments shown in figure 4 is. The papers reads “we can observe a clear decision boundary between the attractive and non-attractive target class. However, the features of the sensitive attribute (gender) are mixed and uniformly distributed, which indicates that the model remains fair.” However I don’t immediately see much difference between MFD as in ME-MFD. It would have helped to have some quantitative measurement (for example the results of a linear classifier on the sensitive attribute) since the qualitative analysis is very difficult.
- The presentation is not always clear and at times I am not sure which algorithm is actually being used (see Clarity section below for completeness), for example:
    - It is unclear what the ME-XXX versions in section 6.1 (Table 1) actually are: is it just multi-exit or is the multi-exit with the additional fairness constraint? One would expect ME-CNN to be the proposed algorithm as shown in Figure 2 but it is actually just the exit strategy proposed by Kaya et al. This is confusing and makes me wonder what all the ME-XXX versions in Table 1 are. How is the proposed method merged with the existing SOTA (i.e., what is the final loss that is optimized? I also looked at the code but unfortunately it did not help me). Also, it would be useful to see there results of ME-CNN with fairness constraint in Table 1.
- The choice of datasets/attributes could be improved:
    - I would avoid using the “attractiveness” attribute to motivate this work, due to its subjectivity and lack of clear definition (what is attractiveness and how was it measured?). I know this was used before but it is always a questionable choice, especially for a paper that deals with fairness.
    - UTK Faces has been collected by crawling the web and most likely without informed consent form. I am aware that this is a widely used dataset but its use still perpetrates a potential injustice, which for a fairness related work is unfortunate.

Minor weaknesses (do not need to be addressed but would improve the paper)
- I think the discussion of why equalized odds is better than demographic parity is unnecessary and potentially wrong. The exact fairness metric that one chooses to adopt depends highly on the task and the objective. There is no better or worst. It is fine to run experiments with equalized odd. In fact, a much better thing to do would be to test the results using different fairness metric and empirically test in which settings early exit can help.
- It is often the case that one of the two deltas (Delta_TPR and Delta_FPR) dominates the other (i.e. it has a much larger magnitude). When combining them as it is done in equation 3 one of them might provides zero signal. One could consider to separate them into two terms each with its own weight for optimization purposes, this separation could also help the analysis.
- The experiments in section 6.2 could be extended to an additional row that shows the multi-exit choice for both scenarios (with and without fairness constraint).
- Clarity could be improved using comments in the section below.

Questions
- Why the alpha coefficients are not learnt?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- Table 1 and 2: bolding results in tables should be done consistently. If one decides to bold the “best” number then all best numbers should be bolded. Currently there is no clear criteria for bolding. This creates confusion and potentially a biased perception of the results.
- Figure 2 does not contain the weight lambda that appears later in the explanation.
- Why presenting the same type of results once with table (Table 1) and once with bar plots (Figure 3)? I’d have bar plots for both and add the tables (for both) in the appendix (or the way around)
- Some parts require more explanation. For example:
    - “In this section, we establish the ablation study of applying a multi-exit training framework to the MFD (Jung et al., 2021).“ While MFD is not propped by these authors since it is used as a comparison in the experiments having some overall information on what MFD does and how ME with the EO additional constraint is applied would help the reader.
    - “As for the fairness regularization loss ls, it is designed to remove the bias between two sensitive groups, such as Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) (Gretton et al., 2012), and Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) (Gretton et al., 2005).” In which sense MMD in Gretton et al was used to remove bias? MMD is a measure between distributions I am not sure I understand what the authors means in this sentence. It might have been used for bias mitigation but I would then cite the work that used MMD rather than the original work where MMD was introduced.
content.summary_of_the_review: The work tackles an important issue: fairness and it seems to be effective and simple. The quality of the explanation (especially the lack of crucial details), however,  and the lack of a more solid empirical section makes it difficult to accept this paper. Even with a great rebuttal I am afraid the amount of changes would require the paper to be re-reviewed.  I do like the spirit of the work so I would encourage the authors to use all the feedback received and make their work more solid for future submission (if this will be rejected).

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes to use intermediate layers' outputs to impose fairness constraints for the task of face attribute classification. The method is very simple. For each residual block, it defines a pair of loss functions for classification and regularization to improve fairness. This paper doesn't clearly say which loss function they used for a fairness constraint, although it was said it could be some of existing methods. I guess they used different loss functions for different experiments. Combined with existing methods, the proposed method was shown to improve classification accuracy and reduce bias (equalized odds).
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
+ This paper studies an important topic in computer vision. 
+ The proposed method is very simple but improves the performance and fairness. 

- Outdated datasets. Both CelebA and UTKFace are very clean datasets. CelebA is a white-dominated dataset (>90%). For the given task, the most popular dataset is FairFace, which contains challenging examples in-the-wild that are well balanced across different sensitive groups. 
- CelebA has 40 attributes. What is the rationale to choose only three out of 40? The complete result for 40 attributes should be reported. 
- There is only one model architecture considered. Does it generalize to other architectures at all? I think there should be more validation on the effect of architecture. 
- There is not much discussion about why this method works. It is not intuitive to understand how this can both improve classification accuracy and reduce bias. For example, any features discriminant to sensitive attributes will be removed early on. How can this improve classification accuracy? Especially, resnet already has skip connections, and some of these effects should be already inherent to some extent. 
- Lots of hyperparameters. How did you choose alpha (0.3, 0.45, 0.6, and 0.9 seem very specific)? There's no explanation about lambda. How did you set lambda? Did you use the same set of the hyperparameters across all the experiments in Table 1? Or was it tuned to specific experiment?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Please see above for clarity. There are lots of missing details.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the method is very simple, but without knowing exactly how this can help improve performance and reduce bias, the result may be accidental. In particular, evaluation is insufficient. I highly recommend that the authors perform additional evaluation to see if their method can generalize under different conditions, using more challenging datasets.

content.title: Fair Multi-exit Framework for Facial Attribute Classification
content.TL;DR: Multi-exit deep neural network improves the model fairness on facial attribute classification.
content.abstract: Fairness has become increasingly pivotal in facial recognition. Without bias mitigation, deploying unfair AI would harm the interest of the underprivileged population. In this paper, we observe that despite the higher accuracy that deeper neural networks can generally offer, fairness conditions deteriorate as we extract features from deeper layers. This phenomenon motivates us to extend the concept of multi-exit framework. Unlike existing works mainly focusing on accuracy, our multi-exit framework is fairness-oriented, where the internal classifiers are trained to be more accurate and fairer. During inference, any instance with high confidence from an internal classifier is allowed to exit early. Moreover, our framework can be applied to most existing fairness-aware frameworks. Experiment results show that the proposed framework can largely improve the fairness condition over the state-of-the-art in CelebA and UTK Face datasets.
